ai.definition: Reinforcement learning agents are artificial intelligence systems that learn to make optimal decisions by interacting with their environment. They receive rewards or penalties based on the actions they take and adjust their behavior accordingly to maximize cumulative reward over time.
ai.howItWorks: These agents use a trial-and-error approach, receiving feedback in the form of rewards or penalties for each action taken. Through this process, they learn an optimal policy that maps states to actions, enabling them to make decisions that lead to better outcomes in complex scenarios.
ai.problemSolved: Reinforcement learning addresses the challenge of decision-making in environments where explicit instructions are not available and the state space is too large for traditional methods like rule-based systems or supervised learning.
ai.manufacturing: Not directly applicable as reinforcement learning agents are software-based AI models, typically developed through programming and training processes rather than physical manufacturing.
ai.buildProcess: The development of a reinforcement learning agent involves defining the environment, setting up the reward function, selecting an appropriate algorithm (e.g., Q-learning, Deep Q-Networks), training the model, and fine-tuning its performance.
ai.costDrivers: Key cost drivers include computational resources required for training, data collection and labeling, and expertise in AI development. The complexity of the environment and the need for extensive testing can also increase costs.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook is positive as reinforcement learning has shown promise across various industries but faces challenges such as scalability and interpretability that need to be addressed.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks are still in development, with varying levels of oversight depending on the application. Privacy concerns and ethical issues related to decision-making processes are areas of focus.
ai.risks: Risks include overfitting to training data, difficulty in understanding and explaining decisions (black-box nature), potential misuse or unintended consequences, and computational inefficiency during training.
ai.profitability: Profitability varies widely depending on the specific application. Successful implementations can lead to significant cost savings and competitive advantages but require substantial investment in both technology and expertise.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments may focus on improving explainability, addressing scalability issues, integrating reinforcement learning with other AI techniques, and enhancing adaptability to dynamic environments.

glossary.def: A type of machine learning where an agent learns to make decisions by performing actions in an environment and receiving rewards or penalties based on the outcomes.
The context in which a reinforcement learning agent operates, providing states and feedback through rewards or penalties.
A mapping from states to actions that dictates how an agent should act in different situations.

subsystems.name: Environment interface
subsystems.role: provides the agent with observations, accepts actions, and returns rewards; may be a simulator or a real system.

subsystems.name: Policy
subsystems.role: the agent's decision-making component: maps observed states to actions.

subsystems.name: Value function / critic
subsystems.role: estimates how good a state or action is, guiding policy updates and reducing variance.

subsystems.name: Replay memory
subsystems.role: stores past transitions so the agent can learn from them repeatedly, especially in off-policy methods.

subsystems.name: Reward function
subsystems.role: defines the objective by assigning a scalar reward after each action; shapes what the agent learns.

subsystems.name: Learning algorithm
subsystems.role: updates the policy and value networks using collected experience.
parts: loss function (e.g., temporal-difference error, policy gradient)

buildSteps.title: Formalise the task
buildSteps.detail: Frame the problem as a Markov decision process: define states, actions, transition dynamics, and a reward signal.

buildSteps.title: Build or choose an environment
buildSteps.detail: Create a simulator or wrap a real system with an interface that steps through time, returning observations and rewards.

buildSteps.title: Design the reward function
buildSteps.detail: Specify rewards that encourage desired behaviour; poorly chosen rewards lead to unintended strategies.

buildSteps.title: Select an algorithm
buildSteps.detail: Choose a reinforcement learning method — for example, deep Q-networks, policy gradient, or actor-critic — suited to the action space and data budget.

buildSteps.title: Implement neural networks
buildSteps.detail: Build policy and value networks using a deep learning framework, matching input and output dimensions to the environment.

buildSteps.title: Set up training infrastructure
buildSteps.detail: Parallelise environment rollouts across many CPU cores or use GPU-accelerated simulators; configure replay buffers and logging.

buildSteps.title: Train the agent
buildSteps.detail: Run episodes, collect experience, and update network weights. Monitor reward curves and adjust hyperparameters.

buildSteps.title: Evaluate and tune
buildSteps.detail: Test on held-out scenarios, check for overfitting or reward hacking, and refine the reward or network architecture.

buildSteps.title: Deploy and monitor
buildSteps.detail: Integrate with the real system, add safety constraints and fallback behaviours, and continue learning cautiously if allowed.

prerequisites.why: they approximate policies and value functions in high-dimensional state spaces such as images or sensor data.
physics simulators enable fast, safe training, but the gap between simulation and reality limits transfer.
training requires millions of environment steps, often accelerated by GPUs or TPUs.
we lack reliable ways to translate complex human goals into reward functions without unintended side effects.
discovering good behaviour in large or sparse-reward environments remains a core research challenge.
deploying learned policies in critical systems requires guarantees that current methods cannot provide.

pathway.milestone: superhuman performance in specific games and simulated control tasks
pathway.unlocks: proof that trial-and-error learning can solve complex decision problems.

pathway.milestone: reliable sim-to-real transfer for robotics and industrial control
pathway.unlocks: automation of physical tasks in warehouses, factories, and agriculture.

pathway.milestone: reinforcement learning from human feedback becomes standard for fine-tuning large language models
pathway.unlocks: AI assistants that better follow human intent and avoid harmful outputs.

pathway.milestone: general-purpose agents that adapt to new tasks with minimal retraining
pathway.unlocks: flexible automation and personal assistants that operate across many domains.

pathway.milestone: reinforcement learning controls complex scientific experiments and systems
pathway.unlocks: accelerated discovery in materials, medicine, and energy.
